biography.name: Priya Menon

background.family: Lives with her father, stepmother, and an older stepbrother; sees her mother on agreed weekends.
background.finances: Stable finances; two households can both support activities but coordination takes effort.
background.geography: Plano, Texas; earlier childhood in Irving.
background.cultureLanguages: English is dominant; understands some Malayalam and uses a few familiar expressions with grandparents.
background.school: Public high school; swim team participant with uneven enthusiasm for academic competition.
background.accessOpportunities: Pool access, supervised safety courses, school resources, and reliable transport when schedules are coordinated.

timeline.story: Priya liked the apartment pool at four but refused to put her face in the water. Her father invented games with floating cups, and she gradually stopped needing him beside every step. At home she replayed animated films and assigned her stuffed animals parts, getting angry when adults changed their voices.

At six she joined lessons with a friend and discovered that she liked repetitive swimming better than the noisy games afterward. She was not the fastest child. Her instructor praised her willingness to try again, but Priya mostly remembers earning a snack and showing her mother the damp paper certificate.

At eight her parents separated. Switching bags between homes became a larger problem than either adult expected, especially when goggles were missing. Swimming remained enjoyable because the pool looked the same every week. She also spent cheerful weekends with cousins, whose elaborate outdoor games rarely involved any organized sport.

At ten she watched a lifeguard manage a minor poolside accident while another adult cleared space. The quiet directions interested her more than the injury. At a later supervised lesson she learned why people should call for trained help and avoid putting themselves in danger. She liked having an ordered first step.

At twelve she completed an introductory safety class using practice equipment and adult instruction. She remembered the sequence on a mannequin but spoke too softly in a paired drill. Her friend was louder and less accurate. Comparing them helped her notice that knowing steps and making yourself heard were separate problems.

At fourteen she swam on a school team and often timed practice laps for teammates. An online swimming group made every small setback sound disastrous, so she muted it during exams. When a teammate became dizzy, she summoned the coach and stayed nearby. The coach handled the situation; Priya felt shaky afterward.

Now sixteen she wants to complete the required training for a supervised pool job next summer if she meets the prerequisites. She likes swimming and concrete safety routines but does not enjoy being treated as the person who must always stay calm. She is practicing a firm speaking voice and still hates shouting across a room.

motivations: Knowing what first step is appropriate
ambitions: Complete eligible pool-job training next summer
supports: Friend who practices speaking with her

biography.selfDescription: I am calm-looking. Inside can be completely different. I like being told exactly what the practice situation is, but real life does not come with that part. I still want the training. Maybe I just want to be at the pool and get paid, which is also true. I do not have a big explanation for why swimming has stayed mine when I dropped so many other activities.
